narration.text: What if this verse isn't about calling someone by a name, but about claiming them as yours?

slides.arabicText: ادْعُوهُمْ لِـَابَائِهِمْ هُوَ أَقْسَطُ عِندَ اللَّهِ فَإِن لَّمْ تَعْلَمُوا ءَابَاءَهُمْ فَإِخْوَنُكُمْ فِى الدِّينِ وَمَوَلِيكُمْ وَلَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌ فِيمَا أَخْطَأْتُم بِهِ وَلَكِن مَّا تَعَمَّدَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَّحِيمًا
slides.translation: Call them to their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah. But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in the system of faith and those under your care. And there is no burden upon you regarding what you erred in thereby, but (there is) in what your hearts deliberately intended. And Allah has always been All‑covering‑in‑forgiveness, Ever‑merciful.

narration.text: Quran 33:5 opens with a command: 'Call them to their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah.' Most readers hear this as an instruction about names. Use the right surname, honor the biological father. The Arabic verb here is from the root dalaynwaw, which appears throughout the Quran meaning to call, to summon, to invoke.

But look at the verse just before this one. It uses the related noun form, those you call as sons, meaning those you claim or adopt as sons. The context is correcting false ascriptions of parenthood. So when this verse says 'call them to their fathers,' it's not about what you call them out loud. It's about who you ascribe them to, who you claim them for. The verb carries the weight of attribution, not just naming. Read this way, the verse draws a line between social bonds and blood lineage, and asks you to honor the distinction.

slides.tagline: A Root Based Translation of the Quran
